description: We are Orbit Origins, a team of innovators from Delhi participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We bring together skills in [coding/design/data science/AI/ML] to solve real-world problems using NASA's open data.
summary: ORBIT ORIGINS tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars for school-age space enthusiasts. We developed a 12-page research paper, a 7-slide cinematic presentation, and a game concept in which players become Mission Archivists who investigate forgotten hardware across seven chapters. The chapters cover Apollo landing sites seen by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, the lost Lunokhod 1 reflector rediscovered in 2010, the Spirit and Opportunity rovers, Apollo and InSight seismology, the effects of dust, signal delay up to Voyager 1 reaching one light-day in November 2026, and how to protect historic landing sites. The project shows that a machine does not stop mattering when it falls silent: it leaves physical, informational, engineering, and cultural legacies. Each chapter turns verified NASA and journal data into a puzzle or decision and ends with the real mission outcome. This matters because it makes real space science approachable, shows how discoveries outlive missions, and encourages young people to explore responsibly.
details:
What it is and how it works
ORBIT ORIGINS is a storytelling project for school-age space enthusiasts about NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. Its core is a game concept in which the player is a Mission Archivist working through a five-step loop: Mystery, Discovery, Interaction, Revelation, and Legacy. Across seven chapters, players investigate real evidence, make a decision or solve a puzzle, then compare their result with the verified mission record. Each finished story is added to a growing archive.

What we developed

  • A 12-page research paper with an abstract, seven case studies, a fact ledger, and 29 sources.
  • A 7-slide cinematic presentation.
  • A full game narrative and storyboards for the seven chapters.
  • The ORBIT ORIGINS logo and visual identity.

The seven chapters
The Moon Remembers (LRO imagery of Apollo sites), The Machine That Vanished (Lunokhod 1, found again in 2010), 90 Days Against Eternity (Spirit and Opportunity), The Worlds Beneath Our Feet (Apollo and InSight seismology), The Invisible Enemy (dust), The Distance Between Two Messages (signal delay, up to Voyager 1 reaching one light-day on 18 November 2026) and The Things We Leave Behind (protecting historic sites).

Benefits and intended impact
The project shows that a spacecraft’s value outlives its mission through four kinds of legacy: physical, informational, engineering, and cultural. It turns real data into hands-on science concepts such as laser ranging, seismic waves, power budgets, and light-time delay. It also asks students to weigh exploration against preserving history.

Tools and methods
Research used NASA and JPL releases and peer-reviewed papers. The paper’s figures and PDF were built with Python (Matplotlib and ReportLab), and the presentation was built as a slide deck. AI tools helped with research support, drafting and design, and the facts were checked against NASA and journal sources.

Creativity
Instead of listing missions, the project treats machines as witnesses and the player as an archivist. A game concept framed as an archive is a different way to tell the story of discarded hardware.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy: every key fact is in a fact ledger with sources and caveats.
  • Scope: Lunokhod 1 is Soviet, not NASA, hardware, so it is framed around NASA’s LRO imagery.
  • Dust: it is not presented as the cause of every failure.
  • Heritage chapter: it is open-ended, with no single correct answer.
  • Time: with limited time, I focused on two polished demo missions first, The Moon Remembers and 90 Days Against Eternity.
